extracted.intended_audience: travelers, students of architecture, architects, and general readers interested in architectural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging and designing ecclesiastical architecture and ornament (with emphasis on St. Mark's / Byzantine vs Gothic issues), focusing on color, scale, material, pictorial decoration, and the relation between domestic and church styles. Useful for critics, architects, and informed travelers assessing fitness of ornament for sacred use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of color: avoid violent colors that confuse perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Violent colors in recesses can 'confuse the architect's eye' and 'injure his perception of more delicate color harmonies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply strong, discordant colors in parts that the eye reads together with delicate tints; consider whether color improves or harms a monument's perception. Antipattern: forcing vivid pigments onto sculptural recesses so as to overwhelm subtler harmonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of color to sculptural character and locality
rubrics_metrics.description: In the South, 'flatness and comparatively vague forms of the sculpture' present conditions that 'set [color] off to the greatest advantage'; breadth of surface displays delicate tints and faintness of shadow joins pearly greys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match chromatic decoration to the sculptural depth and regional character: broad, shallow sculpture benefits from subtle tints and surface color; shallow ornamental tracery may be left white and grounded (e.g., gold or blue) rather than painted naturalistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color should take example from and make use of natural stones
rubrics_metrics.description: Precious marbles give 'the best examples and the best means of color'—their tints are 'exquisite in quality' and permanent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor materials (marble, alabaster, gold, glass) whose intrinsic colors supply durable, subtle harmonies rather than relying only on applied paint. Use natural stone veining and translucency as a palette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt chiselling and ornament to intended viewing distance
rubrics_metrics.description: All good architecture depends upon 'the adaptation of its chiselling to the effect at a certain distance from the eye.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design carvings and details to read correctly at the distance they will be seen from; shallow, delicate reliefs require proximity and will be lost if placed far from the viewer. Antipattern: highly subtle surface sculpture placed too high or too distant to be appreciated.

rubrics_metrics.name: The impression of architecture is not dependent on size
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims of architectural parts depend on 'their delicacy of design, their perfection of color, their preciousness of material, and their legendary interest'—qualities independent of size and 'partly even inconsistent with it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate buildings by quality of detail and material rather than sheer scale; concentrate work where viewers can appreciate minute and beautiful details. Antipattern: assuming grandeur equals goodness; preferring immense mass over refined workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep important decorative work within proximity of the eye
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'delicacy of surface sculpture, nor subtle gradations of color, can be appreciated by the eye at a distance' none of the parts producing such effects 'can be removed far from the eye.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place fine sculpture, subtle color work, and delicate ornament in locations where viewers can approach and inspect them; avoid hiding essential detail on distant buttresses or soaring piers if their value is subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Churches may rightly be richly adorned (fitness of richness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Churches 'ought to be richly adorned, as being the only places in which the desire of offering a portion of all precious things to God could be legitimately expressed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rich ornament and precious materials are defensible for worship spaces as legitimate offerings, provided ornament serves devotional purpose and is executed beautifully. The question to ask is whether the sensation produced aids or distracts from worship, considering the congregation's familiarity with beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess ornament in relation to contemporary domestic architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever Christian church architecture has been good, 'it has been merely the perfect development of the common dwelling-house architecture of the period'—church and dwelling styles were continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ecclesiastical style by how naturally it develops from the common architectural language of its time and place. A noble style should be applicable to both houses and churches; ornament that feels alien to local domestic practice is suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of a noble style: applicability to both dwelling and church
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is the test of a noble style that it shall be applicable to both [dwellings and churches]; for if essentially false and ignoble, it may be made to fit the dwelling-house, but never can be made to fit the church.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A style that works elegantly at multiple scales and uses (domestic and sacred) is likely genuinely noble. Antipattern: a style that functions only for showy convenience in houses but offends when used for worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byzantine style requires pictorial decoration for its large planes
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine work 'leaves void of bold architectural features' and 'requires expression and interesting decoration over vast plane surfaces — decoration which becomes noble only by becoming pictorial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using Byzantine idioms, plan for pictorial (representational) surface decoration—mosaic, painted figures, or natural motifs—because the architecture alone will not fill large plain surfaces effectively. Antipattern: leaving vast Byzantine surfaces blank or attempting to make them architectural in the Gothic manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic style can be effective without pictorial aid
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure Gothic styles are 'capable of filling every vacant space by features purely architectural, and may be rendered ... altogether independent of pictorial aid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor architectural articulation (arches, niches, tracery) where possible if you want an effect independent of pictorial imagery; Gothic can create drama by form alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with beauty conditions whether ornament aids devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: If people are not familiarized with beautiful form and color in daily life, sudden feasting on color and sculpture upon entering a church 'may be a doubtful question' as a preparation for public worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the congregation's habitual visual diet: ornament that delights a population accustomed to beauty will aid devotion; the same ornament may distract or unsettle a population unused to it. Gradual familiarization with beauty is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial religious art's effect depends on viewer's religious disposition and associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of pictorial art on religion varies: Protestants may be offended by art embodying Romanist doctrines, and religious viewers often interpret art through creed and association rather than pure aesthetic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commissioning or placing religious pictorial work, anticipate varied receptions according to doctrinal associations, habits of devotion, and the viewer's prior experiences. Choose subjects and styles mindful of the community's sensitivities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious art ideally narrates accredited truth rather than inventive idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Ever since the Renaissance the painter of religious subject 'is no longer regarded as the narrator of a fact, but as the inventor of an idea'; this shift makes modern religious viewers critical of invention and less credulous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sacred subjects aimed at devotional use, prefer clear, sincere narrational modes that convey accredited truth and avoid overly fanciful invention that may alienate pious viewers. Antipattern: prioritizing artistic invention over intelligible religious narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety in mosaic tesserae and color mixing is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: No two tesserae of the glass are exactly the same tint; greens varied with blues, blues of different depths, reds of different clearness, so that 'the effect of each mass of color is full of variety.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mosaic work should use minute, varied tesserae to achieve shimmering variety and naturalistic nuance; avoid flat, uniform color fields in mosaics if aiming for Byzantine richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat literal vegetal/figure carvings with appropriate natural color; ambiguous ornament can remain abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Where 'oak-leaves and roses were carved into fresh relief and perfect bloom, it was necessary to paint the one green and the other red; but in portions of ornamentation where there was nothing which could be definitely construed... the whole tracery... might be left white, and grounded with gold or blue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paint explicitly representational carvings naturalistically to aid recognition; leave purely abstract or ambiguous ornamental tracery unpainted or treated with harmonizing ground color to preserve architectural rationality.
